en: The Sūtra of the Peerless One, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove.
At the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, [the Buddha] was together with an immeasurable assembly of bhikṣus, immeasurable bodhisattvas, devas, humans, and others.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was sitting alone in a secluded place, reflecting, when this thought arose in him:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a pure heart of faith, takes the three refuges and speaks these words:"

"Now I, [name], take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṅgha, the most honored among assemblies."
"How much merit is obtained by taking such refuge?
Having had this thought, at the rising of the sun, he rose from his seat in his own dwelling, adjusted his robes, and with composed dignity departed for the place where the Tathāgata was.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, bared one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Just now, while I was sitting alone in a secluded place reflecting, this thought occurred to me:
'If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a pure heart of faith, receives the three refuges and speaks these words:'"

"I, [name], now take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṅgha, the most honored among assemblies."
"How much merit is obtained by taking such refuge?
I have not yet understood this; I only pray that the World-Honored One will, out of compassion, explain it for me, so that all sentient beings may attain right wisdom and awakening."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
You possess truly wondrous wisdom; you have been able to contemplate this matter well and have skillfully questioned the Tathāgata regarding this meaning."
"Listen now attentively!
Reflect upon this well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“Yes, indeed,
World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"You should now know this: Jambudvīpa measures seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth; it is broad in the north and narrow in the south, shaped like a carriage box, and the faces of its inhabitants are likewise."

Suppose that within this space they were joined together as a single mass—whether a grove of sugarcane, a thicket of reeds, a bamboo forest, or even fields of rice or sesame—packed so densely that there was no intervening gap.

Suppose, for instance, that the entire continent of Jambudvīpa were completely filled with those who have attained the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), packed so densely that there was no space between them, like a field of sugarcane or similar crops.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to spend a full hundred years making offerings and providing service to all these stream-enterers—honoring and prostrating before them while presenting them with the finest worldly articles of pleasure, such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—[the merit would be immeasurable].

After each and every person who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) has entered *parinirvāṇa*, one shall cremate their body according to the Dharma and collect their relics, erecting a stūpa that is high, vast, and magnificent, and honoring it with various types of ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, flower garlands, exquisite banners, canopies, precious standards, music, and the light of lamps and candles.
"What do you think?
By reason of this cause and condition, would the merit produced thereby not be great?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Very many,
World-Honored One!
Very many!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a pure heart of faith, should speak these words:”

"Now I, [name], take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṅgha, the most honored among assemblies."
"Such sons or daughters of good family will obtain immeasurable merit.

Ānanda, you should know that the merit from the offerings previously described does not equal even one hundredth part of the merit produced by these three refuges; it does not equal even one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor any numerical fraction, nor any calculable fraction, nor any fractional analogy, nor even an *upaniṣad* fraction."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"Set aside for now this continent of Jambudvīpa in the south.

To the east of here lies the continent of Pūrvavideha, which is eight thousand yojanas in length, breadth, and circumference, and is shaped like a half-moon; the faces of its inhabitants are likewise."

Suppose that within this space they were joined together into a single mass—whether a grove of sugarcane, a thicket of reeds, or a forest of bamboo; or perhaps fields of rice, fields of sesame, and so forth—packed tightly together until there was no intervening gap.

Suppose, for instance, that the continent of Pūrvavideha in the eastern direction were entirely filled with those who have attained the fruit of once-returning, packed so closely together as to leave no space between them, like a field of sugarcane.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide offerings and service, including respect and prostrations, for two hundred full years to all such persons who have attained the fruit of once-returning, using the finest worldly articles of pleasure—clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine.

After each and every person who has attained the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*) has entered parinirvāṇa, they shall cremate their bodies according to the Dharma, collect their remains, and erect stūpas that are high, vast, and magnificent. They shall offer praise and worship with all kinds of ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, flower garlands, exquisite banners and canopies, precious standards, music, and the light of lamps and candles.
"What do you think?
By reason of this cause and condition, would the merit produced thereby not be great?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a pure heart of faith, should speak these words:”

"Now I, [name], take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṃgha, the most honored among assemblies."
"Such a son or daughter of good family will obtain even greater merit.

Ānanda, you should know that the merit from the offerings previously described does not equal even one hundredth part of the merit produced by these three refuges; it does not equal even one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor any numerical fraction, nor any calculable fraction, nor any fraction by analogy, nor even an *upaniṣad* (infinitesimal) fraction of it."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"Set aside for now the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha.
As for this western continent of Aparagoyānī, it is nine thousand yojanas in length, breadth, and circumference; its shape is like the disk of the sun, and the faces of its people are likewise."

Suppose that within this space they were joined together as a single mass—whether a grove of sugarcane, a thicket of reeds, or a forest of bamboo, or perhaps fields of rice or sesame—packed so densely that there was no intervening gap.

Suppose, for instance, that the entire western continent of Aparagoyānī were filled to capacity with those who have attained the fruit of non-returning, packed so closely together that there is no space between them, like stalks of sugarcane.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide offerings and support for all such persons who have attained the fruit of non-returning for three hundred full years—with all manner of supreme worldly delights, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—and were to honor and prostrate before them.

After each of those individuals who have attained the fruit of non-returning has entered parinirvāṇa, their bodies are cremated according to the Dharma and their remains are collected. Stūpas are erected for them, lofty, vast, and magnificent, all of which are honored with various types of ointments, powdered incense, and burning incense; with exquisite flower garlands, banners, canopies, precious standards, music, and the light of lamps and candles, they are praised and made offerings to.
"What do you think?
By reason of this cause and condition, would the merit produced thereby not be great?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“Sugata! The Buddha told Ānanda:
“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a pure heart of faith, should speak these words:”

"Now I, [name], take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṃgha, the most honored among all assemblies."
"Such sons or daughters of good family will obtain even more excellent merit.

Ānanda, you should know that the merit from the offerings previously described does not equal even one hundredth part of the merit produced by these three refuges; it does not equal even one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor a numerical part, nor a calculable part, nor a fraction, nor a metaphorical part, nor even an *upaniṣad* part."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"Set aside for now the western continent of Aparagoyānī.
As for this northern continent of Uttarakuru, it is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, its terrain is square, and the faces of its inhabitants are likewise so."

Suppose that within this space they were joined together as a single mass—whether a grove of sugarcane, a thicket of reeds, a forest of bamboo, or else fields of rice, sesame, and so forth—packed tightly together until there was no intervening gap.

Suppose, for instance, that the entire northern continent of Uttarakuru were filled with Arhats—those whose outflows are exhausted and who are free from further afflictions; whose minds have attained mastery and possess right liberation and liberation through right knowledge; whose minds are as well-tamed as great elephants; who have accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, achieved their own benefit, and will not undergo further existence; whose holy life is perfected, and whose bodies and minds are unimpeded; who know the nature of sentient beings, possess the six supernormal powers, and have realized the eight liberations—so densely packed that there is no space between them, like a thicket of sugarcane.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide offerings, serve, honor, and prostrate before all such arhats for four hundred years, using the most excellent worldly articles of pleasure—clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine.

After each and every Arhat has entered parinirvāṇa, they shall cremate their bodies according to the Dharma, collect their remains, and erect stūpas that are high, vast, and magnificent. They shall all offer praise and worship with various kinds of ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, flower garlands, exquisite banners and canopies, jeweled pennants, music, and the radiance of lamps and candles.
"What do you think?
By reason of this cause and condition, would the merit produced thereby not be great?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Very many,
World-Honored One!
Very many!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a pure mind of faith, should speak these words:”

"Now I, [name], take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṃgha, the most honored among all assemblies."
“Such a son or daughter of good family will obtain even more excellent merit.

Ānanda, you should know that the merit from the offerings previously described does not equal even one hundredth part of the merit produced by this threefold refuge; it does not equal even one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor any numerical part, nor any calculable part, nor any fraction, nor any metaphorical part, nor even an *upaniṣad* (infinitesimal) part.”
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"Set aside for now the great continent of Uttarakuru in the north.
Taken as a whole, the four continents are encircled by the Iron Rim Mountains (Cakravāḍa), where one sun and one moon shine."

Suppose that all the mountains and great oceans therein were entirely removed and consolidated into a single expanse, filled to the brim without any gaps—whether by groves of sugarcane, reeds, or bamboo, or by fields of rice, sesame, and so forth.

Suppose, for instance, that throughout the entire Cakravāḍa mountain range, there were Pratyekabuddhas endowed with all the various superior qualities of Arhats, filling it completely and without any gaps, like a field of sugarcane.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide offerings and serve all such Pratyekabuddhas for ten thousand years with the most excellent worldly requisites—clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—and were to honor and prostrate before them.

After each and every one of those Pratyekabuddhas had entered parinirvāṇa, they erected stūpas that were high, vast, and magnificent, and they offered praise and worship with various types of ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, flower garlands, exquisite banners, canopies, precious pennants, music, and the light of lamps and candles.
"What do you think?
By reason of this cause and condition, would the merit produced thereby not be great?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a pure heart of faith, should speak these words:”

"Now I, [name], take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṃgha, the most honored among all assemblies."
"Such a son or daughter of good family shall obtain even greater merit.

Ānanda, you should know that the merit from the aforementioned offerings, when compared to the merit produced by these three refuges, does not equal even one hundredth part of it; it does not equal even one thousandth part; nor does it equal one hundred-thousandth part, nor a numerical fraction, nor a calculable fraction, nor a counted fraction, nor a figurative fraction, nor even an *upaniṣad* (infinitesimal) fraction."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"Setting aside for a moment this single world-system of four great continents, and the area illuminated by one sun and one moon."

Based on this, there is further a small chiliocosm, surrounded on all sides by the Iron Rim Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*). Within it are found a thousand suns and a thousand moons; a thousand great oceans; a thousand Sumeru kings of great jewel mountains; a thousand sets of the seven golden mountain ranges and the Cakravāḍa mountains; a thousand Jambudvīpas, a thousand Videhas, a thousand Aparagoyānīs, and a thousand Kurus; a thousand heavens of the Four Great Kings, a thousand Trāyastriṃśas, a thousand Yāmas, a thousand Tuṣitas, a thousand Nirmāṇaratis, a thousand Paranirmita-vaśavartins, and a thousand Brahmakāyikas. A single Great Brahmā King exercises sovereignty therein; such is called a small chiliocosm.

Based on this, there is further a medium chiliocosm, surrounded on all sides by the Iron Rim Mountains; within it are contained one thousand small chiliocosms, and this is what is called a single medium chiliocosm.

Based on this, there is further a great trichiliocosm, surrounded on all sides by the Iron Rim Mountains; within it are contained one thousand "middle thousand" worlds, which is termed a "trichiliocosm."

Suppose that all the mountains and great oceans therein were entirely removed and consolidated into a single expanse, filled to the brim without any gaps—whether by groves of sugarcane, or groves of reeds, or groves of bamboo, or else by fields of rice and fields of sesame.
Suppose, for instance, that it were completely filled with Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, packed so densely that there was no space between them, like a field of sugarcane.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fulfill twenty thousand years by offering and making offerings of all the most excellent and sublime worldly requisites—clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—to all these Buddhas and Tathāgatas, and were to revere and prostrate before them.

Then, after each of those Buddhas, Tathāgatas, had entered parinirvāṇa, they were cremated according to the Dharma and their *dhātus* were collected. Stūpas were erected—lofty, vast, and magnificent—and all were honored and praised with various kinds of ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, flower garlands, exquisite banners and canopies, jeweled standards, music, and the radiance of lamps and candles.
"What do you think?
By reason of this cause and condition, would the merit produced thereby be great?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were, for twenty thousand years at the abode of a single Buddha, to offer and provide all manner of the world’s most excellent and sublime articles of pleasure—clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—and to honor and prostrate before him.”

After his parinirvāṇa, if one were to cremate his body according to the Dharma and erect a stūpa for the Buddha’s relics—high, vast, and magnificent—and further honor and praise him with various types of ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, flower garlands, exquisite banners, canopies, precious pennants, music, and the radiance of lamps and candles, the merit thereof would already be vast, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable; how much more so the merit produced by making such offerings for twenty thousand years to all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas filling a trichiliocosm? It would be even more immense, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with pure faith, should speak thus:

'Now I, [name], take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṅgha, the most honored among all assemblies.'"
This son or daughter of good family shall obtain even more excellent merit.

Ānanda, you should know that the merit from the aforementioned offerings, when compared to the merit produced by these three refuges, does not equal even one hundredth part of it; nor does it equal one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor a numerical part, nor a calculable part, nor a fraction, nor a metaphorical part, nor even a *upaniṣad* part.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having completed their refuge in the Buddha, having completed their refuge in the Dharma, and having completed their refuge in the Saṅgha, further manages to uphold the ten wholesome actions for even the duration of a finger-snap, by this cause and condition, the merit they obtain will be even more excellent."

Ānanda, you should know that the merit produced by merely taking the three refuges as previously described does not equal even a hundredth part of the merit from practicing the ten wholesome actions for the duration of a finger-snap; it does not equal a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a numerical part, nor a calculable part, nor a comparable part, nor even a fraction of an *upaniṣad* part.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having completed their refuge in the Buddha, having completed their refuge in the Dharma, and having completed their refuge in the Saṅgha, further succeeds in observing the eight precepts for even one day and one night, the merit they obtain will be even more excellent.”

Ānanda, you should know that the merit of the ten wholesome actions performed for the duration of a single finger-snap, as previously described, does not equal even one hundredth part of the merit of the eightfold precepts observed for one day and night; it does not equal even one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor any numerical fraction, nor any calculable fraction, nor any figurative fraction, nor even a *upaniṣad* (infinitesimal) fraction thereof.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having completed their refuge in the Buddha, having completed their refuge in the Dharma, and having completed their refuge in the Saṅgha, further succeeds in upholding the five precepts for as long as they live, the merit they obtain will be even more excellent."

Ānanda, you should know that the merit of the eightfold precepts observed for one day and one night, as previously described, when compared to the merit of observing the five precepts for the duration of one's life, does not equal even one hundredth part of it; nor does it equal one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor any numerical fraction, nor any calculable fraction, nor any fractional analogy, nor even a *upaniṣad* fraction of it.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having completed their refuge in the Buddha, having completed their refuge in the Dharma, and having completed their refuge in the Saṃgha, should furthermore be able to maintain the precepts of a śrāmaṇera or a śrāmaṇerī for as long as their life lasts, the merit they obtain will be even more excellent."

Ānanda, you should know that the previously mentioned merit, compared to this merit, does not equal even one hundredth part of it; it does not equal even one thousandth part; nor does it equal one hundred-thousandth part, nor a numerical part, nor a calculable part, nor a fraction, nor a metaphorical part, nor even an *upaniṣad* part.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"If there should be another who is able to receive and uphold the *śikṣamāṇā* precepts for as long as life lasts, the merit obtained will be even more excellent."

Ānanda, you should know that the aforementioned merit, compared to this merit, does not equal even one hundredth part of it; it does not equal even one thousandth part; nor does it equal one hundred-thousandth part, nor a numerical fraction, nor a calculable fraction, nor a reckoned fraction, nor a metaphorical fraction, nor even a *upaniṣad* fraction of it.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"If there should be another who is able to receive and uphold the bhikṣuṇī precepts for as long as life lasts, the merit obtained will be even more excellent."

Ānanda, you should know that the aforementioned merit, when compared to this merit, does not equal even one hundredth part of it; it does not equal even one thousandth part; nor does it equal one hundred-thousandth part, nor a numerical fraction, nor a calculable fraction, nor a reckoned fraction, nor a metaphorical fraction, nor even an *upaniṣad* fraction of it.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"Furthermore, if there should be one who is able to receive and uphold the great bhikṣu precepts for as long as their life lasts, the merit obtained will be even more excellent."

Ānanda, you should know that the previously mentioned merit, when compared to this merit, does not equal even one hundredth part of it; it does not equal even one thousandth part; nor does it equal one hundred-thousandth part, nor a numerical fraction, nor a calculable fraction, nor a reckonable fraction, nor a metaphorical fraction, nor even a *upaniṣad* fraction.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family can resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and, throughout the limits of the future, uphold the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Pure Precepts without deficiency or transgression, the merit they obtain will be immeasurable and boundless, inconceivable and incomparable, most supreme and most honored, most excellent and most wondrous."

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the Venerable Ānanda received and upheld the Three Refuges and even the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Pure Precepts; the merit he thereby obtained was immeasurable and boundless.
Rejoicing and leaping for joy, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!"
This Dharma gate is most supreme, rare, and inconceivable; it clarifies the profound meaning, and its merit is so vast as to be difficult to measure.
What is its name? How shall I uphold it?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This Dharma-gate is named 'The Peerless. Because it compares and evaluates all kinds of true merits, you should uphold it by this name."
"Why is this so? Because within this sūtra is expounded the most peerless Dharma, which is extremely difficult for all the world to hear.

When the Bhagavān had finished speaking this sūtra, the Venerable Ānanda, the great assembly of bhikṣus, immeasurable bodhisattvas, and the devas, humans, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, and with faith and acceptance, they put it into practice.
The Sūtra of the Peerless One (Anupamā-sūtra)
